extracted.intended_audience: experimental natural philosophers / opticians / members of the Royal Society (scientists studying optics)
extracted.subtask_description: Designing and reporting controlled prism/lens experiments to demonstrate that white light is a mixture of rays of different refrangibility and that colours are properties of rays; includes measurement, control of alternative explanations, and recombination to demonstrate whiteness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Darkened-room prism setup
rubrics_metrics.description: "In a darkened room make a hole in the shut of a window, whose diameter may conveniently be about a third part of an inch, to admit a convenient quantity of the sun's light; and there place a clear and colourless prism, to refract the entering light towards the further part of the room, which... will thereby be diffused into an oblong coloured image."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit apparatus and geometry: small aperture (~1/3 in), clear colourless triangular prism (vertical angle ~60° suggested earlier), place prism at window so refracted spectrum falls on a distant wall; measure image length/breadth and distances. Ensure steady placement of prism and controlled illumination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control for glass irregularities using paired prisms
rubrics_metrics.description: "I took another prism like the former, and so placed it, that the light passing through them both, might be refracted contrary ways, and so by the latter returned into that course from which the former had diverted it... the light... was by the second reduced into an orbicular one, with as much regularity as when it did not at all pass through them."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: attributing spectral elongation to uneven glass. Use two prisms arranged to reverse refraction to cancel contingent irregularities; if irregularities were cause, effects would not cancel. Use paired prisms to test whether observed effects are intrinsic (dispersion) or instrumental.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimentum crucis with apertures and sequential prisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Description of the crucial test: place two boards with small holes (one close behind the prism), a second prism after the second board, rotate the first prism so different parts of the image pass through the second hole, and observe where the second prism refracts those parts on the wall.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designed to show that different parts of the image (rays of different refrangibility) are refracted differently in the second prism — direct operational test that rays differ in refrangibility. Use controlled holes, known distances (~12 feet between boards in original), and systematic rotation to map correspondence between spectral position and emergent direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure geometry and compute refractive power (use sines)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Having made these observations, I first computed from them the refractive power of that glass, and found it measured by the ratio of the sines, 20 to 31..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take precise measurements of distances, image dimensions, angles of incidence/refraction; compute refractive indices using ratios of sines (Snell's-law style computation). Compare computed refractions with observed angular separations to test hypotheses quantitatively. Note potential small discrepancies and revisit hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test alternative hypotheses (incidence variation, thickness, curved ray motion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Newton documents sequentially testing whether spectrum elongation arose from glass thickness, termination/holes, unevenness, differences of incidence, or curvature of rays — e.g., rotating prism to vary obliquity and observing little translation; measuring proportionality of image length to distance; testing for curvilinear ray paths and finding none.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systematically propose and empirically eliminate alternative causes. Rotate prisms, vary aperture sizes, change prism position, and examine proportional relations to rule out incidental explanations. Document negative results as evidence against alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate that light consists of rays differently refrangible (dispersion as cause)
rubrics_metrics.description: "...the true cause of the length of that image was detected to be no other, than that light consists of rays differently refrangible, which, without any respect to a difference in their incidence, were according to their degrees of refrangibility, transmitted towards divers parts of the wall."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show separation of colours by refraction in prism experiments and confirm reproducibly with multiple prisms and measurements. This is the central explanatory criterion: differing refrangibility of component rays explains dispersion and colours.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colours are original/connate properties of rays (not generated by refraction/reflection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposition 1: "Colours are not qualifications of light, derived from refractions, or reflections of natural bodies... but original and connate properties, which in divers rays are diverse."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test by isolating a sort of ray (by separation) and attempting to change its colour by further refraction/reflection or transmission through coloured media — if colour resists change, treat it as a property of that ray. Document repeated failures to alter separated rays' colours.

rubrics_metrics.name: One-to-one correspondence between degree of refrangibility and colour
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposition 2: "To the same degree of refrangibility ever belongs the same colour, and to the same colour ever belongs the same degree of refrangibility... the least refrangible rays... disposed to exhibit a red colour... the most refrangible... a deep violet-colour."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical test: measure refractive deviation for spectral components and observe consistent colour assignment. Use multiple prisms/measurements to confirm that a given refrangibility always corresponds to the same perceived colour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colour species are immutable by ordinary optical interactions
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposition 3 and supporting experiments: "The species of colour, and degree of refrangibility proper to any particular sort of rays, is not mutable by refraction, nor by reflection from natural bodies... nor by any other cause, that I could yet observe... I could never produce any new colour out of it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attempt to change a separated spectral component via refraction, reflection, passage through coloured media, or other manipulations. Robustness (failure to alter) supports the claim. Report all manipulations tried and outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apparent colour transmutations arise from mixtures and separations
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposition 4: "Yet seeming transmutations of colours may be made, where there is any mixture of divers sorts of rays... the component colours appear not, but... constitute a middling colour... when they be again entirely mixed and blended together, they will again compose that colour which they did before separation."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain and demonstrate that mixing spectral components yields composite colours (e.g., blue+yellow→green) and that separating them restores original components. Use fine mixing (or optical recombination) and microscopy to show component persistence in mixtures (example: mixed pigments appear green macroscopically but component colours visible microscopically).

rubrics_metrics.name: White light is a recomposition of all primary spectral colours
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposition 7: "There is no one sort of rays which alone can exhibit this [whiteness]. It is ever compounded, and to its composition are requisite all the aforesaid primary colours... all the colours of the prism being made to converge, and thereby to be again mixed... reproduced light, intirely and perfectly white."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recombine dispersed colours using a lens or reverse-prism arrangement: align prism and lens steadily, transmit all spectral components through a broad lens (object glass ~3-foot radius suggested), intercept at appropriate distance with white paper and observe whiteness. Ensure none of the colours fall beside the lens; move paper to find distance where whiteness is most perfect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical recombination procedure and conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Detailed experimental recipe: place prism at window to form oblong coloured image, then place a lens of about three feet radius at ~4–5 feet from image so colours are transmitted and made to convene at ~10–12 feet; intercept with white paper and move it to and fro to observe colours gradually convene and vanish into whiteness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational guidance: keep prism and lens steady; move paper to find best convergence; note that intercepting any colour at the lens will alter whiteness. Use lens breadth ~2.5–3 inches; prism vertical angle ~60° recommended earlier. Observe inverted order after decussation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of primary and composite colours and mixing rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Propositions 5–6: "There are therefore two sorts of colours. The one original and simple, the other compounded... The original or primary colours are, red, yellow, green, blue, and a violet-purple, together with orange, indigo... The same colours in specie with these primary ones may be also produced by composition: for a mixture of yellow and blue makes green; of red and yellow makes orange..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use spectral series produced by prism as canonical ordering; mixing rules apply primarily to colours not too distant in that series. Note exceptions: widely separated colours (e.g., orange+indigo) do not produce intermediate colours like green.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain natural phenomena (rainbow, coloured bodies) by ray selection and reflection/transmission properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Propositions 10–13: rainbow colours arise because drops refract rays of particular refrangibilities preferentially to the eye; transparently coloured bodies reflect one sort and transmit another so appear differently in different positions, and combined coloured vessels can block all rays when each transmits different sorts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the ray-differentiation model to predict and explain natural optical phenomena: locate which droplets or surfaces will send which refrangible rays to the observer. Test by illuminating coloured objects with uncompounded light to see that they take on the illuminating colour, with relative brightness depending on preferential reflection/transmission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer reflection (reflecting telescopes) to avoid chromatic dispersion if possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation and proposal: "I understood that by their mediation optic instruments might be brought to any degree of perfection imaginable, provided a reflecting substance could be found... and the art of communicating to it a parabolic figure be also attained."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: reflection does not separate rays by refrangibility (angle of reflection equals incidence for all rays), so reflecting optics can avoid chromatism. Practical caveats: reflecting surfaces require extremely fine polishing and shaping because irregularities in reflecting surfaces produce larger stray errors than similar irregularities in refracting surfaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polishing and figure precision requirements for reflecting surfaces
rubrics_metrics.description: "Every irregularity in a reflecting superficies makes the rays stray 5 or 6 times more out of their due course, than the like irregularities in a refracting one: so that a much greater curiosity would be here requisite, than in figuring glasses for refraction."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When attempting reflecting instruments, demand higher precision in surface figure and polish than for lenses; account for amplification of errors and document polishing method and achievable surface tolerances. Consider feasibility given available materials and techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental reporting: document instruments, distances, angles, numeric measures, and negative results
rubrics_metrics.description: Throughout the letter Newton records distances (22 feet, image length 13.5 in, breadth 2.5 in), angles (prism vertical angle 63°12', refractions ~54°4'), computed ratios (sines 20:31), and negative/failed hypotheses (curving rays, glass unevenness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good experimental reporting requires precise numerical specification of apparatus geometry, measured angles and lengths, computed values, and explicit reporting of attempted alternative explanations and their elimination. Include diagrams (figures referenced) and step-by-step procedures to allow reproduction.
